source.title: Diet deep generative audio models with structured lottery
source.authors: P. Esling; Ninon Devis; Adrien Bitton; A. Caillon; Axel Chemla-Romeu-Santos; C. Douwes

record.tranche_reason: The study changes the size of deep generative audio networks through pruning and measures test error, but it does not use an architecture-size sweep or measure the interpolation threshold as in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-error outcomes for pruning levels and selection methods. Its results aggregate across models in places; cited findings about lottery tickets from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a lottery-ticket pruning and compression study of WaveNet, SING and DDSP. It cites Belkin et al. only as evidence that deep models are overparameterized. It never trains models across widths or sizes, never locates an interpolation threshold, and never looks for a second descent. Its test-error-vs-sparsity curves for pruned and retrained subnetworks are a different construct from model-wise double descent. They are aggregated across models and show a single dip then rise, not a fall-rise-fall shape.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that lottery tickets exist in generative audio models, though to a lesser extent than in discriminative tasks. They find that structured trimming works only with global selection, which their mutual-information criterion supports. Smaller trimmed models can be more accurate, and up to 95% of weights can be removed without significant loss. Some light models could fit Raspberry Pi but not Arduino.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates iterative magnitude masking and structured unit trimming for compression, rather than testing the original double-descent model-size, epoch, or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Pruning level and selection method (global versus local; masking versus trimming and choice of criterion) change the reported test-error outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: In aggregate across generative audio models, pruned and retrained subnetworks reach lower test error than the dense model at moderate sparsity (masking minimum 0.893 at 76.1% removed; trimming 0.912 at 80%). Error then rises at extreme sparsity (1.2 at 99% trimmed).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lottery-ticket sparse subnetworks of generative audio models can generalize better than the dense model at moderate sparsity.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Digital Audio Effects (DAFx-20)
record.problems: The reported results are largely aggregate test-error multipliers across different models with different losses and evaluations; the text gives few exact values, and the reported pruning sweeps do not identify an interpolation threshold or provide a complete double-descent curve.
record.rows_left_out: No additional textual test-error outcomes bearing on V1 were omitted. Figure-only curve values were not transcribed where the text did not state their values.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep, no interpolation threshold, no test-error peak or second descent.
No model classes beyond pruned deep networks; nothing past the interpolation point.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V1 limits_scope label is wrong. Pruning sparsity curves are not model-wise double descent, and the paper never frames them that way. Belkin et al. [3] is cited only for overparameterization. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not sweep model size across the interpolation threshold, establish where training data are just fit, or report a complete fall-rise-fall curve.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
The study does not vary the number of training samples to test whether more data raise test error.
The study does not test general double descent across model classes or past the interpolation point.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
The study does not test noise dependence, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not compare complexity measures based on effective parameter counts.

rows.subject: mean test error across different models
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude masking with local selection; 76.1% of weights removed.
rows.measure: test error multiplier relative to the largest model
rows.note: The reported aggregate minimum occurs at this pruning level. It is a point on a pruning sweep, not a complete model-size curve or a measurement relative to an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: A pruning-sparsity point (masking, 0.893 multiplier at 76.1% removed), not a model-size sweep through interpolation. It bears on the lottery-ticket hypothesis, not on V1.

rows.subject: mean test error across different models
rows.operation_detail: Structured trimming with global information-based selection; 80% of weights removed.
rows.measure: test error multiplier relative to the largest model
rows.note: The paper reports this factor for low-pruning trimming. It does not locate an interpolation threshold or establish the full curve.
rows.check: The study's own trimming method, global MI criterion (0.912 at 80% removed). It is a method-performance value, not a double-descent measure.

rows.subject: mean test error across different models
rows.operation_detail: Structured trimming with global information-based selection; up to 99% of weights removed.
rows.measure: test error multiplier relative to the largest model
rows.note: The text reports a factor of 1.2 at 99% removal and says error rises as pruning increases; this is not a complete size sweep.
rows.check: Trimming error multiplier of 1.2 at 99% removed. This is a pruning degradation result unrelated to an interpolation peak.

rows.subject: mean test error across different models
rows.operation_detail: Trimming using the global information criterion; removal level reported as up to 95% of weights.

conditions.value: different audio generative models; aggregate result

rows.measure: test error relative to larger models
rows.value: up to 95% removed without losing accuracy
rows.note: The paper also describes models at this pruning level as 20 times smaller with equivalent quality. No interpolation threshold is identified.
rows.check: The study's own method compared across criteria (95% removed without accuracy loss). It is a compression-performance claim.

rows.subject: mean test error across different models
rows.operation_detail: Trimming with global versus local selection compared across pruning levels.

conditions.value: low pruning, up to 90%, and higher pruning

rows.value: Both selections give lower error at low pruning; global selection gives lower errors up to 90%, then degrades quickly, while local selection maintains its error range at higher pruning.
rows.note: The authors describe these trends but do not provide exact values in the text. The comparison varies pruning selection, not a full model-size sweep through interpolation.
rows.check: Compares global and local selection, i.e. the study's own method variants. No value is given and it has no bearing on double descent.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The introduction cites Belkin et al. as background for overparameterization; the experiments test pruning methods rather than double descent.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates lottery-ticket pruning and compression. It does not measure an interpolation threshold, a double-descent curve, or another listed claim version.

source_check.notes: All five rows describe compression-method performance and should remain excluded from double-descent evidence. The test rationale overstates matters by saying models are never trained across sizes: structured trimming changes size and includes retraining, but does not establish double descent.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: tested pruning levels in the generative audio models
reader_labels.reason: Test error varies with pruning and selection, but these results do not establish the claimed fall-rise-fall curve or peak near just-fitting; see r1–r5.
